..
Issued at 231 PM CST Tue Nov 24 2026

Through Tonight...
A 1035 mb high centered over the Upper Midwest this afternoon 
continues to bring cold, dry, and otherwise fair weather to 
central Illinois. Afternoon temperatures in the low to mid 40s 
will drop into the upper 20s to lower 30s overnight. Increasing 
cloud cover overnight will help limit further radiational 
cooling and keep temperatures from bottoming out further.

Wednesday through Thursday Night (Winter Storm Potential)...
A pair of strong shortwaves are progged to traverse the central
CONUS Wednesday and Wednesday night. A northern stream wave is 
expected to dig across the Dakotas Wednesday morning, while a 
southern stream wave pushes east across the lower Mississippi 
Valley. Model guidance differs slightly on whether these 
features deepen into a pair of closed upper lows (GFS) or merge 
into a single upper low (ECMWF). Regardless of the exact upper-
level evolution, a robust surface response is anticipated, 
featuring a deepening low along the Atlantic Coast and an 
inverted trough pivoting west across Illinois within the 
northwest quadrant of the low.

Precipitation onset is expected as the inverted trough pushes 
westward into the state Wednesday afternoon and evening. 
Although the GFS generates light QPF ahead of the aforementioned
trough, dry low-level air reinforced by northeasterly flow 
should evaporate initial activity into virga earlier in the 
afternoon. As the trough moves into the area, thermal profiles 
initially favor liquid rain as precipitation expands over east- 
central and southeast Illinois. Between 18Z Wednesday and 00Z 
Thursday, the GFS places the 900-800mb layer max wet-bulb zero 
contour roughly along the I-57 corridor (with warmer air to the 
east). Coupled with surface temperatures above freezing, rain is
expected east of this line. While the rain/snow line may wobble
slightly Wednesday night, it will remain near the I-57 
corridor, keeping snow accumulations negligible to the east.

Further west, a corridor of strong frontogenesis will intensify
Wednesday evening and overnight. Dynamic cooling within this
stronger forcing will transition precip to snow by late 
Wednesday afternoon, with thermal profiles supporting snow 
through Wednesday night. Despite a lack of slantwise 
instability, intense frontogenetic forcing should allow snowfall
rates to overcome warm ground/pavement temperatures. NBM 
guidance indicates a 20-30 percent chance of snowfall rates 
exceeding 1 inch per hour at times, primarily across our 
southwestern CWA.

In terms of accumulation, recent GFS runs have shifted 
southwestward, trending closer to the ECMWF solution which 
targets southwestern Illinois with the heaviest snow. Modest 
spread remains regarding the precise axis of maximum totals, 
which will align with the pivot point of the inverted trough. 
The ECMWF places maximum totals closer to St. Louis, while the 
GFS keeps the core slightly further northeast toward central 
Illinois. Given high confidence in the region of model overlap, 
a Winter Storm Watch has been issued. For the ILX CWA, the watch
covers Scott through Christian counties, as well as Cass and 
Menard counties to the north. Within the watch area, 3-6 inches 
of snow appears likely, with locally higher amounts possible if 
heavy snow bands pivot overhead. NBM probability guidance 
highlights a 60-80% chance of 6+ inches of snow in portions of 
the watch area, and a 20-40% chance of exceeding 8 inches. 
Amounts drop off north of I-74 due to shorter precipitation 
duration, and sharply east of I-57 where rain will predominate.

During the day Thursday, the rain/snow boundary will shift to 
the west, changing snow back over to rain across much of the 
area by Thursday afternoon. As temperatures drop Thursday night 
behind the departing system, precipitation may briefly change 
back to snow before ending, though any additional accumulation 
will be minor (a dusting in spots at most).

Friday through the Weekend...
As the upper-level low shifts eastward Friday into the weekend,
flow aloft will become more zonal, promoting a warming trend 
back toward seasonal normals. With the main jet stream 
positioned across the Midwest and Great Lakes, light 
precipitation chances cannot be entirely ruled out. Guidance is 
in better agreement on a fast-moving clipper passing through the
area Saturday night, which could bring a narrow band of light 
rain to parts of central Illinois.
